title: From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Training Must Protect the Seam Between Doing and Thinking · s11-p2】Many of the figures who shaped science, Bacon and Popper among them, insisted that doing and thinking cannot be separated. The data-to-wisdom failures described above occur not within experiment or within theory, but in the translation between them. Whatever its’ institutional form, the aim is only this: to protect the seam between doing and thinking, so that neither experimental rigor nor theoretical depth is euthanized to the pressure for rapid output. These failures, viewed through the DIKW paradigm, each correspond to a broken junction: D→I failures arise when experimental tracks generate data without the statistical discipline to organize it into unambiguous information; I→K failures arise when theoretical tracks lack the empirical grounding to convert structured information into causal knowledge; and K→W failures arise when neither track has the cross-disciplinary reach to abstract universal principles from domain-specific knowledge. Structural reform of scientific training must therefore target these junctions explicitly, not as an abstract ideal but as a concrete design criterion for curricula, collaborations, and evaluation frameworks.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Easy-to-Use Models Demand More Scrutiny, Not Less · s5-p1】The democratization of machine learning and artificial intelligence has provided us with powerful new lenses through which to view our data. However, the ease with which these tools can be applied can occasionally mask the complexity of the underlying mathematics. When the barrier to entry is low, models risk being applied as “black boxes,” without a full accounting of the assumptions built into their architecture. In drug discovery, for example, sophisticated docking algorithms can predict high-confidence binding interactions even when the target protein’s structural integrity has been intentionally compromised or “shredded” in simulation (8). This suggests that, in such cases, the models may respond to sequence-based correlations rather than the fundamental physics of molecular recognition. These instances of non-transferable knowledge remind us that our computational tools are only as robust as the biological, physical, and chemical context we provide. In DIKW terms, this is the I→K transition short-circuited: a black-box model processes inputs into outputs without ever constructing the explanatory causal structure that constitutes genuine knowledge. The result is a system that can reproduce information within its training distribution but cannot generate the understanding needed to reason outside it: pattern without principle, correlation without comprehension.

【Human Judgment Is Indispensable, and Fallible · s6-p1】The same critique applies to the scientists who build and interpret these models. If the ease with which computational tools can be applied masks the complexity of the underlying mathematics, the ease with which a human scientist can reach a simple conclusion equally masks the complexity of the underlying biology. The framework of assumptions needed to turn data into information is a human construction, and it can also be wrong. In this respect, scientists resemble the deep neural networks criticized above: trained on a limited and biased sample of experience, we tend to discount observations that do not fit our expectations and to amplify those that do. This tendency, known as confirmation bias (9), contributes to the poor reproducibility of many published findings (10). Entire fields have been held back for decades because influential figures were confidently wrong. Lipmann’s “squiggle” notation for the “high-energy phosphate bond” (11), popularized in biochemistry textbooks for generations, encouraged the misconception that energy is stored in a particular chemical bond, whereas the free energy released by ATP hydrolysis is a property of the entire reaction, including reactants, products, and solvent. Similarly, when Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty showed in 1944 that DNA is the transforming principle (12), many leading geneticists, including members of the influential phage group, remained unconvinced, in part because the prevailing tetranucleotide hypothesis portrayed DNA as a monotonous polymer too simple to carry genetic information. Nothing in the DIKW hierarchy guarantees that the people climbing it are wise.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Knowledge Is Only as Strong as Its Null Hypothesis · s3-p1】Synthesizing information into knowledge depends on the models used to interpret it, specifically, the null hypothesis that serves as a baseline reference, and the alternative models that could explain the same information. The null hypothesis determines how much knowledge can be gained: a weak one yields little. For instance, positing that a drug binds with extreme specificity to a single protein is easily refuted by many well-designed experiments, so disproving it tells us little beyond the obvious fact that the drug has side effects. By contrast, a null hypothesis that incorporates all plausible alternative explanations yields richer, more precise knowledge about how the drug acts. Too often, studies leave both the null and alternative hypotheses undefined, undermining their reliability. Within the DIKW paradigm, the I→K transition is precisely what a well-constructed null hypothesis operationalizes: it defines the conditions under which organized observations (information) can be forged into explanatory understanding (knowledge).

【A Corrected Marker Is Not a Cured System · s7-p1】The traditional approach to studying biological systems is to develop a mechanistic understanding of the molecular players involved in a particular phenomenon. This approach, while arduous and complex, preserves the causal logic of the processes underlying the phenomenon under study. While the mechanistic approach has yielded a wealth of knowledge, understanding an organism’s function on a grand scale remains elusive. This raises a genuine tension. On the one hand, phenotypic approaches risk mistaking correlation for causation, and mechanistic insight is indispensable; on the other hand, the cell may be so complex that a full mechanistic description is unattainable in practice. Such complexity may make the cell non-separable: its key state variables may not split cleanly into parts that can be measured and manipulated independently, as the classical reductionist program assumes. If so, the problem is not only that the cell is complicated, but that one variable cannot be changed without changing others, as I illustrate in the homeostatic example below. My resolution of the tension is thus not “more mechanism” versus “more data,” but a disciplined hybrid: phenotypic breadth to generate hypotheses, mechanistic depth to test them, and explicit acknowledgment of which coordinates remain unmeasured.
